text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- Coalition government partners seeking compromise in the long-awaited sale of flagship bank Creditanstalt. Conservatives say they want to avoid a breakup of the coalition.
- Federal 1996 budget will be on target even without projected revenues from the sale of Creditanstalt.
- Lack of car stickers required as proof of payment for Austria's newly introduced motorway toll causes avalanche of criticism at home and abroad.
- Creditanstalt supervisory board chief Walther Fremuth sees scope for wide distribution of the bank's shares to individual investors via the bourse.
- Austria has highest share of investment in gross domestic product of all European Union member states, the federal chamber of economy says.
- Duty-free shops on the border between Austria and the Czech Republic will have to close down by mid-year.

- Expert commission submits proposal for new structure of politicians' salaries. According to the proposal, the federal chancellor's annual salary should rise by one million schillings to 3.7 million schillings.

- Social Democrats signal they would be willing to accept Raiffeisen banking group as a key shareholder of Bank Austria once the bank has acquired control of Creditanstalt, creating a new banking giant in Austria.
- Software makers demand stronger legal protection against illegal computer programs.
- New batch of motorway toll stickers will not be available before mid-January, road authorities say. German newspapers pour scorn on Austrian authorities over the toll debacle.

- Privatising Creditanstalt by widely distributing shares to small investors over the bourse is economically unwise since Austrians are traditionally averse to investing their money in equities, says Andreas Woergoetter, head of IHS research institute.
